code.title: Box model: painted width in content-box vs border-box

followUps:
Content-box gives 224px wide; border-box gives 200px. In content-box the 200px is only the content, so you add 10px padding and 2px border on each side: 200 + 20 + 4 = 224px.

In border-box the 200px already includes everything, so the painted box stays 200px and the content area shrinks to 200 - 24 = 176px.

It is not inherited because almost no box-related property is, and the spec keeps it that way so a component can choose its own model. Setting it on html alone would only affect html.

The reset targets every element and its generated boxes directly: *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box }. A variant is html { box-sizing: border-box } *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: inherit }, which lets a widget opt out by setting its own value on its root.

No, outline is not part of the box model. It is drawn outside the border edge and takes no space, so it never changes the size or position of the element or its neighbours.

That is why focus rings use outline: showing a 3px ring does not shift the layout. It may overlap nearby elements, and outline-offset moves it away from the border. Unlike a border, it also follows the shape of the element only in newer browsers and is not per side.

An id rule scores (1,0,0), so it beats any number of classes and can only be overridden by another id rule or !important. Over time this causes escalation: each override needs more weight.

Example: #sidebar .btn is (1,1,0) and beats .btn.primary at (0,2,0), even though the second is more specific to the button. An id also cannot be reused, so the style cannot become a component.

An element can have many classes but only one id. Classes are a space-separated list: class="card featured" matches both .card and .featured.

The id attribute holds a single token; spaces are not allowed in it, so id="a b" is invalid. Two elements sharing one id is also invalid HTML, although browsers will still apply the CSS to both and getElementById returns only the first.

Match the selector's weight and win by order, or move the library into a lower cascade layer. For example, if the library has #nav a (1,0,1), write #nav .item (1,1,0): the class column is compared before the type column, so yours wins.

The cleaner fix is @import url("lib.css") layer(vendor);. Unlayered author styles beat layered ones regardless of specificity, so your plain .item rule wins without an id and without !important.

code.title: Specificity calculator and comparison

followUps:
One id wins. Specificity is compared column by column from the left, so (1,0,0) beats (0,11,0) because the id column is already larger; the class count is never added into it.

Very old browsers wrapped around after 255 classes, but today the columns do not overflow into one another. If you want to override an id rule, use another id, a layer, or restructure the selectors.

It is (0,1,0), the same as a single class. :where() always contributes zero, so #a inside it is ignored and only .b counts.

This makes :where() useful for resets and base styles that must be trivial to override. By contrast :is(#a) would take the weight of its most specific argument, giving (1,1,0).

Layers are compared before specificity, so specificity only decides between rules inside the same layer. A rule in a later layer wins over an earlier layer even with a much weaker selector.

Example: with @layer base, components;, a p { color: red } (0,0,1) in components beats #intro { color: blue } (1,0,0) in base. Unlayered normal rules beat every layer.

The cleanest fix is to make the parent a flex container: the gaps come from whitespace text nodes, and flex items do not create them. Use display: flex; gap: 8px to get exact spacing.

Other options: set font-size: 0 on the parent and restore it on the children, or remove the whitespace in the HTML (or put a comment between tags). Negative margins also work but are fragile because the gap depends on the font.

Images are inline elements, so they sit on the text baseline, and the line box keeps room under the baseline for letters with descenders such as g and y. That leaves a gap of a few pixels under the image.

Fix it with img { display: block }, or vertical-align: middle (or top or bottom). Setting line-height: 0 on the container also hides it but can affect text.

display: contents makes the element generate no box of its own, so its children take part in the layout of the element's parent as if the wrapper were not there.

It is handy for a wrapper that should not break a grid or flex layout: the wrapper's children become the grid items. Its own background, border and padding disappear. Some old browsers dropped semantics of buttons and lists with it, so test with a screen reader.

code.title: em compounds, rem does not

followUps:
Setting 62.5% makes 1rem equal 10px, which makes mental maths easy, but it is controversial because it shrinks everything that was not given an explicit size.

Any text or third-party component that uses the default (16px) now renders at 10px unless every size is rewritten, for example body text as 1.6rem. It does still respect the user's setting, but a simple calc(14 / 16 * 1rem) or a tooling step is safer.

vw and vh are 1% of the viewport width and height. On phones 100vh equals the largest viewport, with the address bar hidden, so a full-height element extends under the visible bar and its bottom is cut off.

dvh is the dynamic viewport height and follows the bar as it shows or hides; svh is the smallest and lvh the largest. Use min-height: 100dvh for full-screen sections.

clamp(min, preferred, max) gives a value that scales with the viewport but never leaves the min and max. Example: font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.5rem + 2vw, 2rem).

At 400px wide: 8 + 8 = 16px (the minimum). At 800px: 8 + 16 = 24px. At 1600px: 8 + 32 = 40px, capped to 32px. Put a rem in the preferred part so browser zoom and user font size still have an effect.

code.title: Cascade resolver: importance, layers, specificity, order

followUps:
Inheritance comes after the cascade. The cascade first looks for any declaration that matches the element for that property; only when none exists does the browser inherit (for inherited properties) or use the initial value.

So an inherited value is the weakest source: a browser rule like a { color: blue } beats body { color: red } for links, even though the link is inside the body.

Important declarations reverse the origin order so that users can always override a site. The order from weakest to strongest is: user-agent, user, author, then author-important, user-important, user-agent-important.

A reader who needs large text or high contrast can write a user stylesheet with !important and the website's own !important cannot beat it. In normal use, user styles come before author styles, so the author wins.

Put the third-party CSS in an early cascade layer, for example @layer vendor, app; and @import url("lib.css") layer(vendor);. Later layers and unlayered styles beat it no matter how specific its selectors are.

Remember that vendor !important flips the order: an early layer's important rule wins. Also avoid raising your own specificity to fight it; scope with a wrapper class or load the library first as a last resort.

code.title: Inheritance and inherit/initial/unset/revert

followUps:
Browsers give form controls their own font in the user-agent stylesheet (for example a system font at 13.33px), so there is a declaration directly on the element and inheritance never applies.

The standard fix is button, input, select, textarea { font: inherit; color: inherit; }. That declaration now matches the control directly and takes the parent's computed values.

all: initial sets every property to its spec initial value, which is not the browser default. A div then becomes display: inline and loses its block behaviour.

all: unset inherits the inherited properties and resets the others to initial; all: revert returns to the browser's styles, which is usually what a clean reset wants. all does not touch direction, unicode-bidi or custom properties.

Yes, custom properties inherit by default, so --gap set on :root is visible in every descendant.

To opt out, register the property: @property --gap { syntax: "<length>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0px; }. Now each element sees only its own value or 0px. You can also reset one locally with --gap: initial.

Sticky usually fails because of one of three things: there is no offset like top: 0, an ancestor has overflow other than visible, or the parent is not taller than the element so there is no room to stick.

See the debugging question for the full checklist. A quick test is to walk up the ancestors in DevTools and look at each computed overflow value and height.

A transform on an ancestor turns that ancestor into the containing block for fixed descendants, so the child is positioned relative to it instead of the viewport. It then also scrolls with it.

filter, perspective, will-change: transform and contain: paint do the same. Typical bug: a modal inside an animated card jumps to the card's corner. Move the modal outside that ancestor, for example to the body or the top layer via <dialog>.

CSS anchor positioning is the modern replacement: give the trigger anchor-name: --btn and the tooltip position-anchor: --btn; position-area: top. The browser places it next to the anchor and can flip it when there is no room.

The Popover API puts the tooltip in the top layer so it is not clipped by overflow. For older browsers a library such as Floating UI computes the position in JavaScript. Plain absolute positioning breaks near the viewport edge.

overflow: hidden makes the element a scroll container, so sticky children attach to it even if it never scrolls. overflow: clip only clips the painting and does not create a scroll container, so sticky keeps looking at the real scroller.

That is why switching an ancestor from hidden to clip often fixes sticky. The trade-off is that a clipped box cannot be scrolled, not even by script, and the property needs a modern browser.

Sticky is cheaper and smoother: the browser handles it in the compositor, with no scroll events, no layout reads and no jank. A scroll listener runs on the main thread on every event and often calls getBoundingClientRect, which can force layout.

You only need JavaScript to react to the stuck state, such as adding a shadow. Use an IntersectionObserver on a sentinel element for that, not a scroll handler.

Make the table's wrapper the scroller and stick the header cells: th { position: sticky; top: 0; background: #fff; z-index: 1 }, with a wrapper such as .wrap { overflow: auto; max-height: 400px }.

Put the sticky rule on th, which is the most reliable. The background is required, otherwise rows show through. With border-collapse: collapse the borders may scroll away, so use border-collapse: separate; border-spacing: 0.

code.title: Margin collapsing rule for two vertical margins

followUps:
A block formatting context (BFC) is a region where the layout of its inside is independent of the outside: margins of children do not collapse through its edge, and it contains its floats.

One is created by: the root html, floats, absolutely positioned boxes, display: flow-root, inline-block, table cells, overflow other than visible or clip, flex and grid items, and contain: layout.

overflow: hidden turned the parent into a new block formatting context. The child's margin can no longer pass through the parent's top edge, so it stays inside and pushes the child down instead of moving the parent.

The side effect is that it clips overflowing content such as shadows and dropdowns. For this purpose use display: flow-root, which creates a BFC with no clipping.

Take the largest positive margin and the most negative one, then add them. Both positive gives the larger; both negative gives the more negative; mixed values add.

Examples: 30px and -10px give 20px; 20px, -5px and -15px give 20 + (-15) = 5px; -10px and -25px give -25px. Negative margins on a block can also pull it over a neighbour, so they are best kept for deliberate overlaps.

Use a clip-based utility that keeps the text in the accessibility tree but not on screen: .sr-only { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; margin: -1px; overflow: hidden; clip-path: inset(50%); white-space: nowrap; }

It does not use display: none, which removes the text from the accessibility tree. The size is 1px rather than 0 because some readers skip zero-size elements, and nowrap keeps the text from being read word by word.

The hidden attribute hides an element by giving it display: none in the browser stylesheet, with the same effect for layout and screen readers.

Because it is only a default rule, any author rule like .box { display: flex } overrides it and the element shows again. A reset [hidden] { display: none !important } avoids that. The value hidden="until-found" lets find-in-page reveal the content.

inert is an HTML attribute that makes a whole subtree non-interactive: it cannot be focused, clicked or selected, and assistive technology ignores it. It is still drawn on screen.

Use it for the page behind a modal, an off-screen drawer or a section that is loading. It differs from display: none, because the content remains visible, and from aria-hidden, which does not stop keyboard focus.

Important declarations use the layer order in reverse: normal rules from a later layer win, but important rules from an earlier layer win. So !important in a reset layer beats !important in components.

Unlayered normal styles beat all layers, but unlayered important styles are the weakest of the important ones. This lets you put a non-negotiable rule, such as an accessibility one, in the first layer.

Utility-first CSS gives flat specificity, no naming work and a CSS file that stops growing, and it keeps values on a shared scale. The costs are long class lists in markup, repeated strings that need extracting into components, a build step, and a learning curve.

Overrides depend on stylesheet order, not the order of classes in the attribute. It suits apps better than a library whose consumers cannot be controlled.

Migrate in steps without a rewrite. 1) Stop the bleeding: add stylelint rules for no new ids or !important. 2) Wrap the old CSS in the first layer, @layer legacy, so any new code wins without specificity fights.

3) Build new components with flat classes in a later layer. 4) Replace legacy by feature and use the DevTools coverage tool to find unused rules. 5) Delete the legacy layer when empty.

code.title: WCAG contrast ratio

followUps:
WCAG 2 contrast ratio is a simple formula that ignores font size, weight and polarity, so it can pass combinations that are hard to read, especially light text on dark backgrounds, and fail ones that look fine.

APCA gives a Lc score that depends on which colour is text, on size and on weight. It is still a draft and not part of the standard, so for compliance keep using the WCAG 2.x ratios, perhaps with APCA as an extra check.

For dark mode, define semantic tokens and swap them under @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark). Add color-scheme: light dark so form controls and scrollbars adapt, and check contrast in both themes.

In forced-colors mode (Windows high contrast) the browser replaces your colours with a system palette, so test with @media (forced-colors: active). Do not rely on background images or shadows for meaning; use real borders and outlines, and system colours such as CanvasText.

prefers-reduced-motion reports that the user asked the operating system to minimise motion, often because movement causes dizziness or nausea.

Respect it: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { * { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; scroll-behavior: auto } }. Better, write big movement only under no-preference, and swap parallax or zooms for a simple fade.

Normal selectors only look at an element and its ancestors, but :has() looks down at descendants and forward at siblings. A change deep in the tree could change the style of any ancestor, which is the opposite of how invalidation normally flows.

Engines needed new data structures to know which ancestors to recheck when a node is added or an attribute changes. They only shipped it after that was fast enough; it is now in all major browsers.

contain: content tells the browser that the subtree is independent, so changes inside it do not force style or layout work outside. content-visibility: auto goes further: it skips style, layout and paint for subtrees that are off screen until they are about to scroll into view.

Pair it with contain-intrinsic-size (for example auto 500px) so the scrollbar does not jump when the real height appears. Large feeds and long articles can see big gains.

Styles in a shadow tree apply only inside it, and outer selectors do not reach in. When a class changes outside, the browser does not need to test the elements inside the shadow tree against the outer rules, and the other way round.

This keeps invalidation local to each component. Inherited properties and custom properties still cross the boundary, and the host can be styled from inside with :host, so theming works through variables.

I would version the tokens, add the new token next to the old one, and keep the old one as a deprecated alias that points to the new value. Lint rules then warn on the old name and a codemod can rename it.

Keep the alias for one or two minor releases, publish a changelog, and run visual regression and contrast tests on the new values. Remove the alias only in the next major version, so no consumer breaks without warning.

Map the library's own variables to your tokens. If it exposes custom properties like --lib-primary, set --lib-primary: var(--color-brand) in a wrapper.

If it has none, load it in a low layer (@import url("lib.css") layer(vendor)) and override in a later layer. Web components expose ::part() hooks. Do not edit node_modules; write a thin adapter component instead.

Choose Tailwind when a small team needs speed and the constraint of a fixed scale, mainly for an application where you control all the markup. It keeps specificity flat and the CSS small.

CSS-in-JS suits styles that depend on props at runtime, but runtime libraries add cost and complicate server rendering, so prefer zero-runtime tools such as vanilla-extract. For a design system used across several frameworks, plain CSS with custom properties is the most portable.

code.title: Why three columns can wrap: percentage arithmetic

followUps:
Use grid: .row { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 16px; }. The fr units share the space left after the gaps, so there is no percentage arithmetic and padding does not cause overflow.

With 600px width and 16px gaps each column is (600 - 32) / 3 = 189.33px. For a responsive version use repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)) so columns wrap by themselves when they get too narrow.

scrollbar-gutter: stable reserves space for the scrollbar even when none is shown, so the content width does not change when a classic scrollbar appears.

Without it, a page that grows taller than the window loses about 15px of width and the layout can reflow, which may wrap a column that fitted before. stable both-edges also reserves the same space on the other side. Overlay scrollbars, as on phones, take no space anyway.

Because 33.34% x 3 = 100.02%, which is 0.02% too much, while 33.33% x 3 = 99.99% fits. On a 600px container the first totals 600.12px, which does not fit, so the last column wraps; the second totals 599.94px.

Browsers snap sizes to fractions of a pixel (1/64px), but the overflow is still positive, so the wrap happens. Using flex or grid with gap avoids the problem entirely.
